definition: Accost means to approach and confront someone aggressively.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word accost. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know accost should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A man with a clipboard accosted me in the parking lot, planting himself between my cart and the car until I heard his pitch.
Anyone can approach you politely to ask the time; approach carries none of the heat that accost promises.
Confront means facing someone directly, even quietly and fairly — it stops short of accost, which rushes an unwilling stranger.

To waylay someone is to stop them mid-route, often by lying in wait along the path they must take. It can even be friendly — a colleague can waylay you by the elevator with good news. Accost is never friendly: the approach itself is aggressive, unwelcome, and forced on its target.

To buttonhole someone is to corner them into a conversation they did not ask for — pushy, but not menacing. Accost is harsher: it carries real aggression, an edge of threat. A chatty neighbor buttonholes you about the fence; a stranger who blocks your path and makes demands accosts you.

To ambush someone is to spring on them from concealment — the surprise is the whole point, and the ambusher hides until the last second. Accost needs no hiding place: the aggressor simply walks up in the open and forces the encounter. Reporters ambush an official from behind a doorway; they accost him face-on in the street.

Accost means to approach and confront someone aggressively.
Halfway up the library steps, the city treasurer was accosted by a stranger who seized her elbow and demanded to know why the fountain was dry; she kept a guard with her after that.
Accost is more than approach and sharper than greet: it names an approach that corners someone — sudden, unwelcome, and edged with aggression.
You approach a teacher after class; you accost someone when you cut off their path and force the encounter.
Accost is the reporter's word for an aggressive, unwelcome approach — stronger than stop or approach, less physical than attack.
If the encounter escalates into a storm of words or blows, you have moved past accost into assail territory (also in this unit).

The night market's security log for June tells one story on repeat.
A man in a gray jacket had been accosting vendors at closing time -- stepping into their stalls uninvited, blocking the till, and demanding 'protection' payments in a low voice.
What unsettled the vendors most, several told officers, was the openness of it: no mask, no shadows, no pretense of browsing.
He would simply walk up, plant himself a foot away, and start making demands.
When plainclothes officers finally stood behind a fruit stall on the 30th, he approached them the same way -- and was arrested mid-sentence.
